content: Why does looking up one product become slow when the products table gets large? I thought an index was a general speed switch, so once the table has one, every search should become fast automatically.

An index is closer to a sorted guide than a general speed switch. It helps when the query searches or orders by the columns recorded in that guide. An index on product_id may make one product lookup quick, while a search on color can still scan every row. The database also decides whether using an available index is actually cheaper.
What does it mean for the index to be on a column? I pictured one index sitting beside the whole table and pointing to anything a query might ask for.

Each index stores chosen column values in an organized structure, along with references to the matching table rows. If it stores product_id, it can navigate by product_id, but it has no ordered map of color values. You can create separate indexes or a multi-column index, though each one takes space and must be maintained when data changes.
So why does the database sometimes ignore an index that matches the search box? Is that a mistake, or can reading the entire table genuinely be the quicker route?

Reading the table can genuinely be quicker when a condition matches a large share of its rows. Following an index means reading index entries and then fetching table rows, often from many scattered locations. A sequential scan can read the table in a simpler pass. The query planner estimates both costs from table statistics and chooses the lower estimate.
What should I check when a product search stays slow, then? I would otherwise keep adding indexes until one happens to make the query quick.

Start with the query's execution plan. It shows whether the database scans the table, uses an index, sorts rows, or spends time elsewhere. Check the exact filter and sort columns, how many rows match, and whether statistics are current. Add an index only when that evidence identifies a useful access path; then measure the query again.

What is the real difference between giving a database more memory and adding an index? They seem equivalent to me, because both let the database keep the information closer and avoid slow disk reading.

They solve different problems. More memory lets the database cache frequently used pages, reducing physical disk reads. An index changes how rows can be found, providing an organized route to a small subset. A fully cached table may still require examining millions of rows, while an index may navigate to a few matches without examining the rest.
Why would examining rows in memory still matter if memory is fast? I assumed the waiting time came entirely from moving data off the drive, not from checking the data itself.

Memory is fast, but scanning millions of rows still consumes CPU time, memory bandwidth, and often time comparing values or evaluating conditions. It can also displace other useful pages from the cache. An index reduces the amount of work. More memory reduces the cost of some reads; those benefits can complement each other, but they are not interchangeable.
Suppose the entire customers table fits into memory. Would an index on email still help, or does fitting the table into the fast area make that index pointless?

An email index can still help substantially. Without it, the database may compare the requested email with every customer row, even if all rows are cached. With a suitable index, it navigates through a much smaller structure to the matching entry. The difference may shrink compared with a disk-bound scan, but it usually remains meaningful as the table grows.
Then why does adding memory sometimes fix a slow query without any new index? Does that mean the query was organized correctly and only its pages were being fetched repeatedly?

That is one possibility. If the query already uses a sensible access path but repeatedly waits for index or table pages from disk, a larger cache can help. Memory can also improve sorting and joins by keeping temporary work out of disk files. The execution plan and read statistics distinguish an access-path problem from an I/O or working-memory problem.
What evidence would separate those cases clearly? I can compare runtimes, but a faster second run seems vague because the first run may have warmed everything up.

Compare execution plans with actual row counts, buffer or page-read statistics, and temporary-disk usage. A large scan examining far more rows than it returns suggests an index opportunity. Many physical reads that disappear on a warm run suggest caching. Disk-based sorts or hash operations suggest insufficient working memory. Test repeatedly under representative load, because an isolated warm query can mislead.
Why did adding several indexes make saving orders slower? Indexes make database work faster, so having more of them should help inserts and updates as well as searches.

Indexes mainly accelerate particular reads. When a row is inserted, the database must also add entries to every relevant index. An update may remove and replace entries when indexed values change, and a delete must remove them. More indexes therefore create extra writes, logging, page changes, and sometimes contention, so write operations can become slower.
What exactly gets written into each index when an order is added? Is it another full copy of the order, or just a small address pointing back to it?

Typically an index entry contains the indexed value, a row locator or primary-key value, and some structural overhead. It is not usually a full row, although included columns can make entries larger. The database must place that entry in the index's ordered structure and record the change safely, which is more work than storing one tiny pointer.
Why can changing a delivery note be slow if the note is not indexed? I would expect unrelated indexes to stay untouched when their column values do not change.

The exact behavior depends on the database and table design. Some systems can update a non-indexed column without changing index entries, while others may create a new row version and update pointers or perform cleanup later. Triggers, constraints, transaction logging, and page space also contribute. The plan for locating the row and write metrics can reveal which part is costly.
Does that mean I should remove every index that is not used daily? That seems safe, because a rare report can simply take longer when someone requests it.

Not automatically. A rarely used index might support an important monthly report, a uniqueness rule, a foreign-key operation, or an emergency lookup. Usage counters also reset after restarts and may miss seasonal work. Review each index's purpose, read benefit, maintenance cost, and overlap with other indexes before removing it, then monitor the affected queries.
What is an overlapping index in ordinary terms? If one list is for customer and another is for customer plus date, I assume they are completely separate tools.

They are separate objects, but their usefulness may overlap. An index ordered by customer, then date can often support searches by customer alone because customer is its first key. In that case, a customer-only index may be redundant, though it is smaller and could still be cheaper. Column order, included values, uniqueness, and actual plans determine whether consolidation is sensible.
Why does the first key matter for that decision? I thought the database could enter a two-part index through either part and then follow the nearby entries.

A typical multi-column B-tree is sorted first by the first key, with the second key sorted only inside equal first-key groups. It resembles a phone book ordered by surname and then given name: finding a surname is direct, but finding every particular given name requires scanning many surname sections. Some databases have alternatives, but that ordering rule is the useful default.
What is the point of choosing an order for a two-column index? If both name and city are inside it, the database should be able to search either one equally quickly.

A common B-tree index is arranged lexicographically: first by its leading column, then by the next column within matching leading values. An index on city, name can quickly locate one city's range and then one name inside it. Searching only by name leaves matching names scattered across all city ranges, so the same index may help much less.
Why not store both arrangements automatically when I create the index? It is still the same pair of columns, so I assumed reversing them would cost almost nothing.

The reversed arrangement is another complete index structure, not a free second view. It duplicates keys and row references in a different order, consumes storage and cache, and must be updated on every relevant write. Some workloads justify both orders, but the decision should come from actual search patterns rather than the mere presence of two columns.
Suppose most searches provide both city and name, while a smaller group provides only city. Which order is sensible, and what happens when only the second box is filled?

City, name is a reasonable candidate because it supports both-column searches and city-only searches through its leading key. When only name is provided, the database may scan the index, use a different index, or choose a table scan. Confirm with execution plans and data distribution; a highly selective name-only search may justify its own index.
What if city has only a few possible values but name has many? I am unsure whether the first column should be the common one or the one that narrows results most.

There is no universal rule that the most selective column must come first. Equality filters on both columns can often use either order efficiently, while prefix searches, ranges, sorting, and queries that omit one column make order important. Choose the order that serves the broader query pattern, then use real plans and measurements rather than selectivity alone.
Why is a search for active accounts still slow after indexing the active flag? An index speeds every filtered query, and this filter is about as simple as a filter can be.

An active flag usually has only two values, and one may match most rows. If ninety percent of accounts are active, the index points to nearly the entire table. Fetching those rows through many index references can cost more than reading the table once, so the planner may correctly ignore the index. How much a condition narrows results matters.
What is this narrowing property measuring? Is it just the number of different values in a column, or the share of rows returned by this particular search?

Both ideas are related but distinct. Cardinality describes how many distinct values a column has. Selectivity usually describes how small a share a condition matches. A two-value flag has low cardinality, yet searching for a rare false value could still be selective. The planner uses statistics about frequencies, not merely the count of distinct values.
Then why might the same active index help when I ask for inactive accounts? It feels inconsistent for one value to use the index and the other value to skip it.

The two values can have very different frequencies. If inactive accounts are one percent of the table, the index offers a short route to that small group. If active accounts are ninety-nine percent, scanning is cheaper. A cost-based planner can choose different access methods for the same prepared query, depending on available statistics and parameter handling.
Would combining the flag with a date make the index useful for active accounts? I mean an index containing active status and the day the account was created.

It can help when queries filter active status and a sufficiently narrow date range, because the pair may identify far fewer rows. Column order should match the query forms: status then date supports an equality on status followed by a date range. If queries usually filter only by date, leading with status may limit reuse, so inspect the full workload.
What is a filtered index, and would it be cleaner to keep only active rows in one? I assume a smaller list always gives the fastest possible active-account query.

A filtered, or partial, index stores entries only for rows meeting a condition. It can be compact and useful for a minority state, such as only inactive or pending accounts. Indexing the majority active state may still be large. It is not automatically fastest: the query must imply the index condition, and result size and needed columns still affect cost.
Why would the query need to imply the condition if the words look equivalent to a person? Could active equals true and not inactive be treated differently by the database?

The optimizer must prove that every row needed by the query is present in the partial index. Simple equivalent expressions may be recognized, but parameters, null values, functions, or more elaborate logic can prevent that proof. For example, not inactive behaves differently when inactive is null. Matching the indexed predicate plainly makes use more reliable and preserves correct results.
What should I record before deciding whether this flag index is worth keeping? Query time alone seems incomplete if the index also affects writes and memory.

Record which queries use it, their frequency and latency, rows matched versus rows examined, and plans for common flag values. Also measure index size, cache pressure, and write volume on the table. Check whether a composite or partial index would serve a narrower need. Evaluate under representative data, since a nearly even flag can become heavily skewed later.
What does a full table scan actually do when I search for one invoice number? I assumed the database sees the column name and jumps directly to that part of the table.

A table is not normally arranged into separate physical sections for every column. Without a usable index on invoice number, the database reads table pages and tests the condition against rows until it has covered the required data. Even if only one row matches, it generally cannot know where that row is without an organized lookup structure.
Why can it not stop after finding the invoice? Invoice numbers are supposed to be different, so the first matching row should prove there cannot be another one.

It can rely on uniqueness only when the database has an enforced constraint or unique index proving that property. A naming convention or application promise is not enough. Even then, without a structure locating the value, it may scan until it finds the row; the uniqueness proof can allow stopping at that point, but the match might be near the end.
Is the primary key already an index, or must I add a second index for the same invoice number? I see both words used and they sound like separate features.

In most relational databases, declaring a primary key creates or requires a unique index that enforces and supports it. You usually should not add a duplicate index on the identical column order. There are product-specific details about clustered storage and constraint backing, so inspect the table definition and existing indexes before creating another one.
What would the query plan show if the invoice lookup is working properly? I want a plain sign that it reached a small part instead of checking everything.

Look for an index seek, index scan over a very narrow range, or similarly named indexed access using the invoice condition. Compare estimated and actual rows: both should be close to one for an existing unique invoice. Page or buffer counts should also be small relative to the table. Exact labels vary by database, so focus on access path and work performed.
Why might it still scan even after I add the right invoice index? My first guess would be that indexes are simply unreliable on a table that has grown too large.

Large size usually makes a selective index more valuable, not less. A scan may persist because the query transforms the column, compares incompatible data types, uses a leading wildcard, has stale statistics, or returns many rows despite its appearance. Confirm that the plan's condition matches the indexed expression and that the supplied value has the same type as the column.
Why does sorting recent messages take time when there is already an index on the message table? An index keeps things ordered, so any requested order should come out ready-made.

An index keeps its own key columns in a particular order, not every column in every possible order. An index on message_id cannot directly supply created_at order. Even an index on created_at may not fit a query that first filters by conversation. An index ordered by conversation_id and created_at can often support both that filter and that ordering.
What happens during the separate sort the plan mentions? Does the database copy all matching messages somewhere else and rearrange them before returning the first page?

Conceptually, yes: it gathers the values or rows needed by the next operation and orders them. If the working set fits in the memory allowed for sorting, that can be quick. If it does not, the database may write temporary runs to disk and merge them. A limit can reduce work in some plans, but not always eliminate the sort.
Would an index on created time alone fix the page that shows one conversation? I assume the database can read newest entries first and discard messages from other conversations as it goes.

It can do that, but it may inspect many unrelated recent messages before finding enough from the chosen conversation. A composite index beginning with conversation_id and continuing with created_at groups the relevant messages together in time order. That usually gives a more direct path, especially for conversations with sparse activity among a large global message stream.
Why does descending order sometimes appear in an index definition? If an index is ordered, reading it backward should always provide the reverse order for free.

Many databases can scan a B-tree backward, so a single-column ascending index often serves descending output too. Direction becomes more important with mixed ordering, such as category ascending and score descending, where simply reversing the scan reverses both columns. Database capabilities differ, so compare the requested ordering with the complete index definition and plan.
What changes when two messages have the same created time? The display still needs stable pages, but the time index seems unable to decide which one belongs first.

Add a unique tie-breaker to both the requested order and, when useful, the index—for example, order by created_at and message_id. That produces deterministic ordering when timestamps match. It also supports keyset pagination using the last timestamp and identifier, avoiding the growing skip cost and shifting-page behavior associated with large offset values.
What should the final index look like for newest messages in one conversation, using that tie-breaker? I want to understand the column sequence rather than copy a magic command.

The usual shape is conversation_id first, because the query selects one conversation, followed by created_at and message_id in the requested ordering. The database can enter one conversation's range and read a stable newest-first sequence. Include other displayed columns only after measuring whether avoiding table lookups outweighs the larger index and additional write cost.
What makes a join between customers and orders slow? Both tables already have indexes, so the database should connect matching rows quickly no matter which columns the join uses.

Having indexes somewhere on both tables is not enough. The join columns and the number of matching rows matter. If orders.customer_id is indexed, the database can efficiently find orders for selected customers. If only order_date is indexed, that does not map customer identifiers. The optimizer may also prefer a hash or merge join when many rows participate.
Why would the customer side need an index if customer ID is already marked as the primary key? I was planning to add another ordinary index there for the join.

The primary key is normally already backed by a unique index, so another identical index is usually redundant. The commonly missing piece is an index on the referencing side, such as orders.customer_id. A foreign-key declaration does not create that index in every database. Check existing definitions rather than assuming either that it exists or that both sides need duplicates.
What is the database doing when it chooses a hash join instead of following the customer index repeatedly? The word hash sounds like another kind of permanent index.

A hash join usually builds a temporary in-memory lookup table from one input, keyed by the join value, then probes it with rows from the other input. It is an execution technique, not normally a permanent stored index. For large, unsorted inputs it can be cheaper than performing thousands of separate index lookups, especially when many rows will be returned.
How can I tell whether indexing the order-side customer number will help this join? The result shows many orders, but the starting customer filter is fairly small.

Inspect the actual plan and row counts. If the database first finds a small set of customers, then repeatedly searches orders by customer_id, that order-side index can be effective. Compare rows examined, page reads, and runtime before and after. If nearly all orders qualify, a sequential scan plus hash join may remain cheaper despite the new index.
Why does searching names that contain a word ignore the name index? Since the letters are in the index, I am certain every kind of text search should use it.

A normal B-tree index is ordered from the beginning of each value. It can efficiently find a known prefix, such as names starting with mar, because those entries occupy a contiguous range. A contains search with a leading wildcard can match the word anywhere, scattering matches throughout the index, so the database may need to scan it all.
What is the practical difference between starts with and contains here? They both compare letters, so I do not see why moving the percent sign changes the route.

With starts with, the first characters establish where the matching range begins and ends in alphabetical order. With contains, the unknown beginning prevents that navigation. It resembles a dictionary: finding words beginning with river is direct, while finding every word containing river requires checking entries unless you build a different guide organized for internal pieces.
Would adding more memory make the contains search equivalent to having that different guide? If the names remain in memory, checking all of them seems like the same shortcut.

More memory can make the scan cheaper by avoiding disk reads, but it does not create a route to the matching substrings. The database still examines many values and performs comparisons. A text-search, trigram, or similar specialized index stores searchable pieces in an organized form. Which type fits depends on the database and the matching behavior you need.
What is a trigram in ordinary terms, and why can it find letters in the middle? I am picturing every name being copied three times, which seems too simple.

A trigram is a sequence of three neighboring characters. A specialized index records many such sequences from each value and maps them back to matching rows. A search term supplies its own trigrams, which narrow the candidate rows before the full condition is checked. It stores more than three copies, so the speed benefit comes with meaningful storage and write overhead.
Does that specialized index make every text query faster, including exact names and very short searches? I would replace the normal name index if one structure covers everything.

No single text index is best for every pattern. A B-tree is often excellent for exact equality, ordering, and prefixes. A trigram-style index helps many substring and similarity searches, but very short terms may provide too little information, and the index is larger. Some systems can combine paths, but keeping or replacing indexes should follow the actual query mix.
Why does changing names to lowercase inside the search sometimes prevent the normal index from working? The stored letters are the same apart from capitalization, so that seems harmless.

An index on the raw name values is ordered by that stored expression and its collation rules. Applying a function can create a different expression whose order is not represented by the index. Depending on the database, use a case-insensitive collation or data type, or create an expression index on lower(name), then write the condition to match it.
What measurements would show that the new text index is worthwhile rather than merely larger? I need something more specific than seeing one search finish quickly once.

Test representative exact, prefix, substring, short-term, and no-match searches against realistic data. Record median and tail latency, rows rechecked, buffer reads, index size, build time, and added insert or update cost. Examine plans to verify the intended index is used. Include concurrent traffic, because a larger index may compete with other data for cache space.
What is a covering index, and why would it be faster than an ordinary one? I believed an index already contained whatever the query needed from the matching row.

An ordinary index reliably contains its key values and a way to locate the table row, not necessarily every column the query returns. A covering index contains all columns needed for that query, either as keys or included values. The database may then answer from the index alone, avoiding separate table-page fetches for each match.
Why not include every column so the index covers every query? That should make every read faster, and storage seems like the only cost of the extra copies.

A very wide index consumes more storage and cache, takes longer to scan, and increases write work whenever included data changes. Large text or document fields can make it especially bulky. It may also overlap other indexes without helping their search order. Covering works best as a targeted optimization for important, frequent query shapes rather than as a duplicate table.
What is the difference between a key column and an included column? If both are stored in the same index, I would expect either one to guide the search.

Key columns determine the index's searchable order and can support filters, ranges, joins, and ordering according to their sequence. Included columns are payload stored with entries so results can be returned without visiting the table; they generally do not establish navigation order. Exact syntax and capabilities differ, but that key-versus-payload distinction is the central idea.
How can the plan prove that the table was not visited? I see an index name in the plan, but that alone does not tell me what happened afterward.

Look for product-specific signs such as index-only scan, covering index, or the absence of a table lookup operator. Runtime page statistics can confirm few or no heap or base-table reads. Some databases still visit table metadata to check row visibility, so index-only does not always mean literally zero table-related work. Measure rather than relying solely on the operator's name.
When would covering make almost no difference even though the plan can use it? I assume avoiding one extra trip per row should always be a major improvement.

The gain can be small when very few rows are fetched, table pages are already cached, rows are physically nearby, or another operation dominates the query. A wider covering index may even require more pages than a narrow index plus a handful of table lookups. Its benefit grows when many scattered lookups are avoided, but the complete plan determines the result.
Why can a query be fast the second time without changing its index? I take that as proof that adding RAM is the same improvement as adding an index.

The second run often benefits from cached table and index pages, plus cached operating-system data. That removes physical reads but does not change how many rows or pages the plan examines. An index can reduce that work by creating a better access path. Caching and indexing may both lower runtime, yet they change different parts of the process.
What does a cold query mean, then? Is it simply the first query after restarting the database, or can parts of the needed data remain warm in other places?

Cold usually means the needed pages are absent from relevant caches, but achieving a truly cold test is difficult. The database buffer pool, operating-system cache, storage controller, and remote storage layers may each retain data. A restart may clear only some layers. That is why production-like repeated measurements and page-read counters are more informative than one supposed cold run.
Would it be sensible to size memory so every table stays cached and stop creating indexes? Scanning cached data sounds predictable, while indexes add several structures to maintain.

That can work for small datasets and modest workloads, but it scales poorly. Cached scans still consume CPU and memory bandwidth, and concurrent scans compete with one another. They also push useful pages out as data grows. Selective indexes reduce the quantity of data processed, while sufficient memory keeps those useful index and table pages readily available.
Why might an index itself fail to stay in memory? I imagined it as a tiny list of pointers, so even a large table's index should fit easily.

Index entries include key values, row locators, structural data, and free space for future changes. Wide keys, multiple indexes, and billions of rows can make indexes substantial. Only frequently accessed portions may remain cached. Internal upper levels are often small and hot, while leaf pages holding most entries move in and out depending on workload and memory pressure.
What comparison would fairly test more memory against a new index? Running each option once seems likely to favor whichever one inherits a warmer cache.

Use repeatable datasets and workloads, multiple runs, and the same cache conditions for each case. Record plan shape, rows examined, logical reads, physical reads, CPU time, and latency distributions. Test concurrent activity and writes too. The goal is not merely choosing a winner: it is identifying whether the bottleneck is excessive work, physical I/O, insufficient sort memory, or contention.
What does it mean when the database estimates that half the rows will match? If an index exists for the filter, I thought the estimate should not affect whether it gets used.

The estimate strongly affects the choice. An index is attractive when it leads to a small portion of the table. If half the rows are expected, following index entries and fetching their rows may cost more than a sequential scan. The optimizer compares estimated costs, using statistics about value frequencies, table size, page layout, and available access paths.
Why can that estimate be far from the actual number? The database owns the table, so it should know exactly how many times every value appears.

Keeping exact counts for every value combination would consume space and make every change more expensive. Databases usually maintain sampled summaries, distinct counts, histograms, and selected frequent values. Those summaries can become stale or miss relationships between columns. Parameters and expressions add uncertainty. Statistics trade perfect knowledge for manageable planning overhead.
What is a histogram in this setting? I picture a chart, but I do not understand how a chart tells the planner whether to read an index.

It is stored statistical information that divides a column's value range or frequency distribution into buckets. The planner can use those buckets to estimate how many rows satisfy conditions such as price below a threshold. That estimated row count feeds the cost comparison between an index path and alternatives. It need not draw a visible chart during planning.
Would refreshing statistics force the query to use the index? I assume a fresh count should make the indexed route clearly best because the index is already available.

Refreshing statistics can correct a poor estimate, but it does not guarantee index use. Accurate statistics may confirm that a scan is cheaper. They may also expose skew or table growth that changes the choice. After refreshing, compare estimated and actual rows and inspect the selected plan; success means a well-informed choice, not a particular operator.
Why do two filter columns cause worse estimates than either one alone? If the database knows each column's numbers, multiplying them should give the combined answer.

Multiplication assumes the columns are independent. Real data often violates that assumption: postal code and city, for example, are strongly related. Estimating them separately can predict combinations that rarely or never occur. Some databases support extended or multi-column statistics to capture such dependencies. Rewriting conditions or selecting a composite index can help, but first verify the estimation error.
What is the safest response when estimated rows and actual rows are very different? Adding another index feels like the direct fix, since indexes speed up every query eventually.

Treat the bad estimate as a planning-information problem first. Refresh statistics, inspect skew, check parameter values and data types, and consider extended statistics where supported. An additional index may offer a good path, but the optimizer can still misuse or ignore it when estimates are wrong. Fixing the estimate can improve several operators, join orders, and memory decisions at once.
Why does an index help with prices between two amounts? I understood indexes as shortcuts for exact matches, so a range seems as though it should still check every price.

A B-tree index keeps price keys in sorted order. The database can navigate to the first key at the lower boundary, then read neighboring entries until it passes the upper boundary. It checks only that contiguous slice rather than every price. The benefit depends on how large the slice is and whether many table rows must then be fetched.
What happens if the range includes most products? The index is still sorted correctly, so I assume it remains faster than reading the unsorted table.

Correct ordering does not guarantee lower cost. If the range contains most products, the database may traverse much of the index and then fetch most table rows, possibly in scattered order. A sequential table scan can read fewer total pages more predictably. The planner estimates the matching fraction and may switch methods as the boundaries change.
Why does adding category before price help a search within one category? Could the database not use the price index first and remove products from other categories afterward?

It can use price first and filter category afterward, but it may examine many irrelevant entries. An index on category, price groups each category's prices together. With category equality and a price range, the database enters the chosen category, navigates to its lower price, and reads only that category's bounded slice. That often reduces index and table work.
What if the query uses two ranges, such as price and created date? I expect a two-column index to narrow both ranges in the same direct way.

A typical ordered index can usually navigate efficiently through equality keys and then one range dimension. Once it scans a price interval, created dates are ordered only within each exact price value, not globally across the interval. The second condition may be checked as a filter. Choose the sequence based on selectivity, sorting, and query patterns, then inspect the plan.
What is the downside of placing an index on every column? Since indexes speed up every query, covering all columns separately seems like the safest setup for unpredictable searches.

Separate indexes on every column consume disk and cache, slow inserts, updates, and deletes, extend backups and maintenance, and may still not match multi-column filters or ordering. Low-selectivity columns can offer little read benefit. The optimizer can sometimes combine indexes, but a deliberate smaller set shaped around important query patterns is usually more effective than blanket indexing.
Why does each index make a delete slower? Once the main row is gone, I assumed its little pointer in an index could simply be left there and ignored.

Leaving stale entries would waste space and could produce incorrect lookup candidates unless every read performed extra checks. Databases remove or mark index entries as part of the transaction, then may reclaim space later. Each index therefore adds page changes, logging, locking or versioning work, and cleanup. The precise timing differs, but the maintenance cost is real.
What does index bloat mean? Is it merely unused disk space, or can empty gaps in the index actually make searches take longer over time too?

Bloat generally means the index occupies more pages than its useful entries require, often after churn, page splits, or delayed cleanup. Extra pages use disk and cache and can increase the work of scans. Point lookups may be less affected, but a larger structure still has costs. Database-specific maintenance tools can measure and sometimes rebuild or compact it.
Should indexes be rebuilt on a fixed schedule to keep them fast? Weekly rebuilding sounds harmless and guarantees the lists remain neatly packed at all times.

A fixed rebuild schedule can waste resources, generate heavy I/O and logs, block or compete with normal work, and provide no benefit when bloat is small. Some databases manage fragmentation differently or offer lighter maintenance. Measure index size, page density, scan performance, and workload impact, then use the product's recommended maintenance based on evidence rather than a universal weekly rule.
How do I decide which similar indexes to keep? For example, one starts with account, another with account and date, and a third adds status afterward.

Map each index to actual filters, joins, ordering, and returned columns. The longer indexes may serve account-only lookups because account leads, but they are larger and may differ in uniqueness or coverage. Review execution plans and usage over a representative business cycle, estimate write cost and size, and remove redundancy cautiously while monitoring queries that relied on the smaller path.
Why can a smaller duplicate-looking index still win if the longer one begins the same way? I thought the shared beginning made their lookup speed identical.

The smaller index fits more entries on each page, uses fewer cache pages, and may require less reading for a scan. It can therefore be cheaper even with the same leading key. Conversely, the longer index may cover a query and avoid table visits. Shared prefixes create overlap, not identity; measurements show whether consolidation helps overall.
What is a sensible first step before deleting one of those indexes? I want evidence that includes rare queries without waiting indefinitely for every possible report.

Document the index's constraint role, review query plans and usage statistics across a known reporting cycle, and search application queries for its leading columns. Account for monitoring resets and seasonal jobs. If your database supports making an index invisible or unusable reversibly, test that under representative load; otherwise remove it only with a rollback script and focused monitoring.
Why does filtering by the year of an order date stay slow when order date has an index? The query uses that column directly, so the index should speed it up automatically.

A condition like year(order_date) equals 2025 applies a function to each stored date. A normal index is ordered by complete date values, not by the function's result, so some optimizers cannot navigate it directly. Writing a bounded date range—at least 2025-01-01 and before 2026-01-01—often exposes a contiguous index range.
What makes the range version different if both versions describe exactly the same year? I assumed the database would rewrite obvious date wording before choosing its route.

Some optimizers perform certain rewrites, but they cannot safely or universally transform every function, data type, time zone, or null behavior. Explicit boundaries state the searchable interval in the same values the index stores. This property is often called sargability: the condition presents a search argument the access structure can use for navigation.
Would an index on the year expression solve it without changing the query? That sounds strictly better because the stored list would contain the exact answer the filter asks for.

An expression or generated-column index can help that exact filter, where the database supports it. It is not strictly better: the year has few distinct values, a popular year may match many rows, and the new index adds maintenance. A regular date index also supports narrower months, days, ranges, and ordering, making it more broadly useful.
Why would comparing the date to a piece of text also interfere with the index? The text looks like a date, so conversion should be a harmless detail.

Implicit conversion must occur on one side. If the database converts the indexed date column for every row, its stored order may no longer provide the needed search path; conversion can also change semantics or fail. Use a correctly typed date parameter and unambiguous boundaries. Then verify the plan, because conversion rules differ among database products.
What should I look for in the plan to recognize this kind of hidden conversion? A scan tells me something failed, but not which part caused it.

Inspect the predicate details, not only the scan operator. Plans often show a cast, conversion, or function wrapped around the indexed column, sometimes under a residual filter rather than an index condition. Compare parameter and column types in the schema. Warnings, estimated rows, and rows removed by filtering can provide further evidence that navigation was lost.
